title: P-values and Carrying Out a Test for a Population Proportion
videoTitle: AP Statistics Topic 3.6 & 3.7 P-values and Carrying Out a Test for a Population Proportion
intro: After this lesson you can calculate the test statistic for a one-sample $z$ test for $p$, find and interpret the p-value, compare it with $\alpha$, and write a conclusion in context.

moments.title: What a test is trying to show
moments.text: The goal is to find evidence for the alternative hypothesis. The two possible conclusions are evidence or a lack of evidence.

moments.title: Restaurant takeout claim
moments.text: $H_0: p=0.60$, $H_a: p>0.60$. In a random sample of 250 customers, 170 ordered takeout, $\hat p=0.68$.

moments.title: Samples vary
moments.text: A sample proportion means little until you compare it with all the sample proportions you could get.

moments.title: PHANTOM steps
moments.text: Parameter, Hypotheses, Assess conditions, Name the test, Test statistic, Obtain the p-value, Make a decision.

moments.title: The null distribution
moments.text: Assume $H_0$ is true and build the sampling distribution of $\hat p$ centered at $p_0$.

moments.title: Test statistic
moments.text: $z=\dfrac{\hat p-p_0}{\sqrt{p_0(1-p_0)/n}}$ tells you where $\hat p$ falls in the null distribution.

moments.title: Beyond 2 standard deviations
moments.text: A $z$ beyond about $\pm2$ is unusual if the null is true.

moments.title: The SD is built on $p_0$
moments.text: The whole sampling distribution assumes the null proportion is true, so the standard deviation uses $p_0$.

moments.title: P-value
moments.text: The probability, assuming $H_0$ is true, of a result as extreme as or more extreme than the one observed.

moments.title: Normal distribution in Desmos
moments.text: Plus, Inference, Probability Distributions, Normal with mean 0 and SD 1, then Cumulative Probability.

moments.title: Two-sided alternative: double it
moments.text: For $H_a: p\ne p_0$, find one tail and multiply by 2.

moments.title: Smaller p-value, stronger evidence
moments.text: The lower the p-value, the more convincing the evidence for $H_a$.

moments.title: Significance level
moments.text: $\alpha$, usually 0.05 or 0.01, is the cutoff for statistically significant.

moments.title: Reject $H_0$ does not mean $H_0$ is false
moments.text: Say there is convincing evidence for $H_a$, not that you proved it.

moments.title: Never conclude $H_0$ is true
moments.text: Fail to reject means there is not convincing evidence for $H_a$.

moments.title: Conclusion in context
moments.text: State it in terms of $H_a$, in context, with non-definitive language.

moments.title: Dog park: full test
moments.text: 361 of 465 residents want the park. Is that convincing evidence that more than 75% do?

moments.title: z test for proportions in Desmos
moments.text: Enter successes and sample size, choose the test, enter $p_0$ and the tail.

moments.title: Dog park conclusion
moments.text: The p-value is above 0.05, so fail to reject $H_0$: not convincing evidence that more than 75% want it.

moments.title: Pick the correct test statistic
moments.text: Numerator $\hat p-p_0$, and the SD uses $p_0$, not $\hat p$.

cards.name: p-value ≤ α
cards.text: Reject $H_0$. There is convincing evidence for $H_a$.

cards.name: p-value > α
cards.text: Fail to reject $H_0$. There is not convincing evidence for $H_a$.

notes.label: Wording check.
notes.text: The video describes tests as "proving" the alternative and says the restaurant sample "should not have occurred." On the AP exam, say the result would be very unlikely if $H_0$ were true, so there is convincing evidence for $H_a$. A test never proves either hypothesis.

sections.title: Carry out the test
sections.intro: A full test follows the PHANTOM steps from the video. This lesson adds the last three.
steps: Assess conditions: random, 10%, and large counts using $np_0\ge10$ and $n(1-p_0)\ge10$.
Name the test: one-sample $z$ test for $p$.
Obtain the p-value from the standard normal distribution, in the direction of $H_a$.
Make a decision by comparing the p-value with $\alpha$, then conclude in context.

parts.label: Center
parts.text: The null distribution assumes $H_0$ is true.

parts.label: Observed
parts.text: The sample result we are judging.

sections.title: Null distribution explorer
sections.intro: Set $n$, $p_0$ and the number of successes. The curve is the null distribution of $\hat p$, and the shaded tail is the p-value. Simulate samples to see where it comes from.

stories.rest: A restaurant chain claims more than 60% of customers order takeout. In a random sample of 250 customers, 170 ordered takeout. $H_a: p>0.60$.
stories.bulb: A company claims fewer than 8% of its light bulbs are defective. In a random sample of 650 bulbs, 42 were defective. $H_a: p<0.08$.
stories.remote: A school board believes the share of parents who support remote learning is different from 50%. In a random sample of 300 parents, 141 support it. $H_a: p\ne0.50$.
stories.dog: A city will build a dog park only if more than 75% of residents want it. In a random sample of 465 residents, 361 want it. $H_a: p>0.75$.

sections.title: Desmos walkthrough
sections.intro: The calculator starts empty. Work through each task in it yourself, the way you would on the exam, then check what you observe.

steps.title: Test statistic by hand
steps.suppose: we want $z$ for the restaurant: 170 of 250 customers, $p_0=0.60$.
steps.observe: The value is positive because $\hat p$ is above $p_0$, and it is beyond 2, so the sample is unusual if $H_0$ is true.

steps.title: Right-tail p-value
steps.how: tap the plus button, choose Inference, then Probability Distributions, then Normal with mean 0 and standard deviation 1. Open Cumulative Probability, choose the right option and enter 2.582.
steps.observe: Only a sliver of the curve is shaded. Open the dropdown for more decimals.

steps.title: Left-tail p-value
steps.suppose: we want the p-value for the light bulbs: 42 of 650 defective, $H_a: p<0.08$.
steps.how: find $z$ with (42/650-0.08)/sqrt(0.08*0.92/650), then use Cumulative Probability with the left option.
steps.observe: The tail is on the left because $H_a$ uses $<$. The video rounds $\hat p$ to 0.0646 and gets $z=-1.453$; small differences come from rounding.

steps.title: Two-sided p-value
steps.suppose: we want the p-value for remote learning: 141 of 300, $H_a: p\ne0.50$.
steps.how: find $z$, use the left option for $P(Z\le z)$, then multiply that value by 2 on a new line.
steps.observe: Doubling counts results this far from 0.50 in either direction.

steps.title: The whole test in Desmos
steps.suppose: we want Desmos to do the dog park test: 361 of 465, $H_0: p=0.75$, $H_a: p>0.75$.
steps.how: tap the plus button, choose Inference, then the z test for proportions. Enter 361 successes and 465 for the sample size, create the test, choose the hypothesis test, enter 0.75 and choose the right tail.
steps.observe: Desmos reports $z$ and the p-value without rounding. The $z$ is positive because 361/465 is above 0.75.

steps.title: Report the decision
steps.suppose: Desmos gives the p-value for part of a free-response question.
steps.how: compare it with $\alpha=0.05$ and write the decision and conclusion in context.
steps.observe: A bare p-value does not earn credit. Show the comparison and the conclusion.
steps.expected: Because $0.0948>0.05$, fail to reject $H_0$. There is not convincing evidence that more than 75% of all residents want the dog park.

sections.title: Write it so it earns credit

traps.title: Saying the test proves $H_a$
traps.weak: This proves more than 60% of customers order takeout.
traps.better: Because the p-value of 0.0049 is less than $\alpha=0.05$, we reject $H_0$. There is convincing evidence that more than 60% of all the chain's customers order takeout.

traps.title: Accepting the null hypothesis
traps.weak: We accept $H_0$: half of parents support remote learning.
traps.better: Because the p-value of 0.299 is greater than $\alpha=0.05$, we fail to reject $H_0$. There is not convincing evidence that the proportion of all parents in the city who support remote learning differs from 0.50.

traps.title: Interpret the p-value
traps.weak: There is a 0.0049 probability that $H_0$ is true.
traps.better: Assuming 60% of all customers order takeout, there is about a 0.0049 probability of getting a sample proportion of 0.68 or higher in a random sample of 250 customers.

traps.title: Using $\hat p$ in the standard deviation
traps.better: In a significance test the standard deviation uses the null value: $\sqrt{0.35(0.65)/200}$.

questions.stem: For the restaurant test of $H_0: p=0.60$ against $H_a: p>0.60$, the p-value is 0.0049. Which is the correct interpretation?
opts: There is a 0.0049 probability that 60% of customers order takeout
Assuming 60% of all customers order takeout, there is a 0.0049 probability of getting a sample proportion of 0.68 or higher by chance
There is a 0.0049 probability that more than 60% of customers order takeout
why: A p-value is not the probability that a hypothesis is true. It assumes $H_0$ is true.
It is a conditional probability: assuming $H_0$, how likely is a result at least this extreme.
The p-value says nothing directly about the probability of $H_a$.
The p-value is not a proportion of customers.

questions.stem: A city claims 40% of residents bike to work. In a random sample of 150 residents, 51 bike to work. Which is the test statistic for $H_a: p<0.40$?
why: The standard deviation in a test uses $p_0=0.40$, not $\hat p$.
The numerator is backward: it should be $\hat p-p_0$.
$\hat p=51/150=0.34$, minus $p_0$, over the standard deviation built from $p_0$. This gives $z=-1.5$.
The denominator uses $n=150$, not $n-1$.

questions.stem: A test of $H_0: p=0.25$ against $H_a: p\ne0.25$ gives $z=1.80$. What is the p-value?
why: That is one tail. A two-sided test doubles it.
That is $P(Z\le1.80)$, the area on the wrong side.
That doubles the two-sided p-value again.

questions.stem: A test gives a p-value of 0.032 with a significance level of $\alpha=0.01$. Which conclusion is correct?
opts: Reject $H_0$; there is convincing evidence for $H_a$
Fail to reject $H_0$; this shows $H_0$ is true
Fail to reject $H_0$; there is not convincing evidence for $H_a$
why: 0.032 is greater than 0.01, so the result is not significant at this level.
Failing to reject never shows that $H_0$ is true.
The stated level is 0.01. You compare with the $\alpha$ you were given.
0.032 > 0.01, so fail to reject, and say there is not convincing evidence for $H_a$.

questions.stem: Why does the standard deviation in a one-sample $z$ test for $p$ use $p_0$ instead of $\hat p$?
opts: The test assumes $H_0$ is true, so the null distribution is centered at $p_0$ with a standard deviation computed from $p_0$
$\hat p$ is not known until after the sample is taken
Using $p_0$ always gives a smaller standard deviation
The large counts condition requires it
why: Every part of the null distribution comes from assuming $H_0$, including its spread.
$\hat p$ is known when you compute the test statistic. Confidence intervals do use it.
It can be larger or smaller depending on the values.
The large counts check in a test also uses $p_0$, but that is not why the formula uses it.

sections.title: Write a full response
sections.prompt: A school district of 9,000 students claims that more than 70% of its students eat breakfast before school. A reporter takes a random sample of 120 students; 92 say they eat breakfast before school.
parts: (a) State the hypotheses and define the parameter.
(b) Check the conditions for a one-sample $z$ test for $p$.
(c) Calculate the test statistic and the p-value.
(d) At $\alpha=0.05$, what should the reporter conclude? Answer in context.
sample: (a) $H_0: p=0.70$ and $H_a: p>0.70$, where $p$ is the proportion of all students in the district who eat breakfast before school.
(b) Random: the students were a random sample. 10%: 120 is less than 10% of 9,000 students. Large counts: $120(0.70)=84\ge10$ and $120(0.30)=36\ge10$.

(d) Because the p-value of 0.056 is greater than $\alpha=0.05$, the reporter should fail to reject $H_0$. There is not convincing evidence that more than 70% of all students in the district eat breakfast before school.
checklist: (a) Correct hypotheses with the parameter defined in context
(b) Checks random, 10% and large counts, using $p_0$ for large counts
(c) Test statistic about 1.59 with the standard deviation built from $p_0$
(c) P-value about 0.056 from the right tail
(d) Compares the p-value with $\alpha=0.05$ and fails to reject $H_0$
(d) Conclusion in context about $H_a$, with no claim that $H_0$ is true

flags.text: At 1:27 the video says tests are about "proving" the alternative. The page uses "convincing evidence" and shows a wording note.
At 23:00 the video says the restaurant sample "should not have occurred." The page says it would be very unlikely if $H_0$ were true.
At 21:30 the captions say "the null proportion of 68%"; the null is 60% and 68% is the sample. Check the audio.
At 42:39 the captions say Desmos gives "negative 1.312" for the dog park. The correct value is $z\approx+1.312$, since 361/465 is above 0.75. The page uses the positive value.
Desmos menu names (Inference, Probability Distributions, z test for proportions) come from the captions and are unconfirmed against the current calculator.
Light bulbs: the video rounds $\hat p$ to 0.0646 and gets $z=-1.453$; the page computes from 42/650 and gets $z\approx-1.446$, p-value $\approx0.0741$. Confirm 42 defective bulbs on screen.
New explorer: one-proportion-test. Check the presets and the simulation in class.
